html:
The map's label for the island of Hawaiʻi in 1492, under the name of the later Hawaiian Kingdom, Kō Hawaiʻi Paeʻāina. In 1492 there was no kingdom of all the islands yet. The island of Hawaiʻi, the largest, was ruled by chiefs (aliʻi), and tradition places the high chief Līloa at his court in Waipiʻo valley around this time.

Polynesian voyagers had settled the islands centuries before (settlement of East Polynesia). Hawaiian society was strictly ranked and bound by sacred rules, the kapu, which lasted until 1819. It was fed by irrigated taro terraces, fishponds and sweet potato fields.

Līloa's son ʻUmi-a-Līloa is remembered as the chief who first united the whole island under one rule, around 1500. Island rulers fought each other for the next three centuries, until Kamehameha I, a chief from this island, conquered the others between 1795 and 1810 and founded the Kingdom of Hawaii.
